title: How 40 ships beat 46: Nelson's square-law trick
description:
In a gunfight every ship shoots and every ship gets shot, so a fleet's strength goes with the square of its size (Lanchester's square law, 1916). Line 40 ships against 46 and it's 1,600 against 2,116: you lose and about 23 of theirs survive. Nelson's plan for Trafalgar cut the enemy line instead: 32 ships on 23 is 1,024 against 529, nearly two to one, and the survivors plus the other 8 then beat the remaining 23. At Trafalgar on 21 October 1805, 27 British ships of the line broke a line of 33; 18 French and Spanish ships were captured or destroyed and the British lost none.

Numbers checked in code (the square-law arithmetic, plus 100,000 simulated battles each way). Sources: Lanchester, Aircraft in Warfare (1916), ch. 6, en.wikisource.org/wiki/Aircraft_in_Warfare_(1916)/Chapter_6 ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trafalgar ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanchester%27s_laws

beats.say: Your 40 ships against 46. One plan loses, one wins.
Same ships, same guns, same sailors. Only the arithmetic changes.
This was Nelson's plan at Trafalgar, in 1805. In 1916, Frederick Lanchester showed why it works.
Every ship shoots, and every ship gets shot. Double your fleet, and you fire twice as much, at an enemy whose shots are spread twice as thin. That's 4 times the strength.
So square it. 40 squared is 1,600. 46 squared is 2,116. Line against line, you lose, and about 23 of theirs sail home.
Same 40 ships. How do you flip that?
Cut their line in half. Throw 32 ships at 23 of theirs. 1,024 against 529, nearly two to one. You win, with 22 left.
Now bring in your other 8. 30 against 23, and you win again, with about 20 ships still afloat.
At Trafalgar, Nelson's 27 ships broke a line of 33. 18 of theirs were taken or destroyed. Britain lost none.
